## Preferences

Claudinite self-test: 7 probes passed. # Owner interaction preferences Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](../packs/) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase. ## Preferences - **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does. - **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md](../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`. - **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc. - **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control. - **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.) - **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of. - **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes. - **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked. # Claudinite — active-pack guidance The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand. # Working discipline The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project. Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better. Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Put the class **alone on that line**: the line is scanned for *every* class token on it, so restating the menu to rule options out ("not a correction, feature request, or process-change") declares all of them, arming the gates those classes carry. Any explanation goes on the next line. This cannot be taken back — the transcript is append-only, and a clean re-declaration further down does not override the first. 1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule. 2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes. 3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Put on the ladder only a rule that constrains *how work is done* and outlives any one feature; a checkable signature doesn't earn a rule its place. Reject two shapes outright: a check that asserts particular code exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time — it dies with the code it pins and constrains no later change), and a rule derivable from the product's requirements (that is a requirement — take it to mode 2: the requirements document and the test that proves it). Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it. The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for. Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided. When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs. When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix." Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out. Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere. Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet. When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change. An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action. # The task lifecycle The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill. For every new task: 1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work. 2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`). 3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done. --- # HTML Portable, project-agnostic practices for hand-authored HTML — semantic markup, accessibility, forms, and the document structure pitfalls that recur regardless of framework — true for any HTML read cold. - **Injected block markup inside a `

` silently empties it — read the sibling, not the tag.** When a `

` is filled with raw HTML (e.g. `innerHTML`, or a framework's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html` / `ng-bind-html`), a block element inside it (a `

`, etc.) is disallowed by the HTML content model, so the parser (browser or jsdom, same rule) auto-closes the `

` right before it and the injected content lands as the `

`'s **next sibling**. Read `element.nextElementSibling`. - **An ambiguous numeric slash date can't be resolved from its digits — infer the document's convention once, don't guess per-field.** When both parts are ≤ 12 (e.g. `05/07/2026`), resolve the order once per document — never per source or per field — in this order. (1) **An unambiguous sibling date fixes the page's convention**: a slash date elsewhere on the same page with a part > 12 (e.g. `24/07/2026`) parses only one way, and a page is almost always internally consistent — read that date's order and apply it to every other slash date on the page. (2) Failing that, **read the declared locale** (``, `og:locale`): default **month-first** (the order `Date` and most JS parsers assume) and flip to day-first only on a *positive* non-US signal — a non-US region in `lang` / `og:locale`, or a non-English language; a bare `en` with unknown region stays month-first. The `.` / `-` separators are day-first regardless. - **When code must react to how a real page actually behaves, investigate it live before you ship — don't deploy a hypothesis you can only test after release.** If a change hinges on the real DOM, computed styles, or runtime state of a page you can't see, hand the user one JavaScript snippet to run in the browser DevTools console and read its output back. Reserve "test it after it's deployed" for behavior you've verified genuinely can't be observed now. - **Make that console request a snippet, not an essay.** Send exactly one code block to paste into the console and ask the user to paste its output back. Skip the prose explaining what you're hoping to learn. --- # product-wiki — the self-growing product research wiki This project keeps its market/user/competitor research as a self-growing wiki under `product-wiki/` (Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern: compile findings once, refine in place). Layout, required page sections, the Key insights header's shape, growth-log dating, source links, staleness, and the isolation wall are **check-enforced** — the finding is the instruction, so this prose never restates them. The full growth procedure is the pack's task doc (`packs/product-wiki/tasks/wiki-growth/task.md`). - **Every page opens with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a few bullets carrying the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the competitor that already does this, the thing that turned out not to be true — enough that a human who reads only the header understands what was researched and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing and competitors"), not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to. - **Terse, plain, and only the non-obvious.** One short line per bullet, in ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, no jargon a newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would *surprise* someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the number nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point is obvious is genuinely hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep it**. A borderline-obvious line costs the reader two seconds; a long, careful line costs them the header. - **The header is a current view, not a log.** A pass that changes what a page's most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded insight leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below), and an insight the pass didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's top-line understanding, the header doesn't move. - **The sink is human-reviewed only.** `product-wiki/product-requirements/` never changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and waits for a human. It is the only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may build on. - **Compile once, refine in place.** Read the target page end to end before researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as open, thin, or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass. Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current. - **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source), never deleted without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's growth log and updates the open questions in both directions. - **No fabricated growth.** Most passes find little or nothing; no new citable material → no edit, no log entry, no PR. - **sample-data and new wikis.** `product-wiki/sample-data/` gains a file only when a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test asserts against belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/` outside the two reserved names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so create one only deliberately, seeded with its required sections; automation refines existing pages, it never invents new ones. - **Review discipline.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR — researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate. The owner phrase **"grow the product wiki"** runs the worker method in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR discipline. --- # tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills ([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md), [single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md), [single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)). The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.** - **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete; **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a ref's auto-generated name. - **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive. Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites **its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body. --- # claudinite-website This repo's own conventions: the `site/` marketing page and the upkeep of this repo's vendored Claudinite mount. ## Rules - **The site describes itself in prose — a behaviour change must correct every self-description it falsifies, in the same commit.** `site/index.html`, `site/privacy.html`, the header comment in `site/assets/style.css` and `site/README.md` all make checkable claims about what the site loads, collects, and deploys, and nothing fails when a change quietly makes one of them untrue. Adding the analytics beacon (#36) left the privacy lede's no-tracking claim and the stylesheet's "No external assets" standing, and took a second commit to walk both back; dropping the deploy workflow's `paths:` filter (#45) left `site/README.md` still saying the site publishes only on a push that touches `site/**`. Before landing a change to site behaviour or to `deploy-pages.yml`, grep the site copy, the CSS/JS header comments and `site/README.md` for what the change makes false, and ship the correction (and any disclosure the behaviour requires) in the same commit as the behaviour. - **Adopting an *additional* canon pack is not a local lookup — the vendored `.claudinite/shared/packs/` holds only what this repo already adopted, never the catalog of what's adoptable.** Nothing in the checkout lists the available packs, and the `adopt-claudinite` skill's canonical pointer (`bootstrap.md`) is *not* vendored here, so it can't be read locally either. Don't exhaustively grep the tree to prove a pack is missing: shallow-clone the canon (`missingbulb/Claudinite`) to scratch, list `packs/`, and pick from there. Then declare the pack in `.claudinite-checks.json`, vendor it with the canon checkout's `vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs --target . --ref ` (never hand-copy pack files), scaffold whatever the pack's own rules require, and delete the scratch clone. **Match the owner's plain-words name to a pack id before asking them to disambiguate** — the names differ ("the market research pack" is the `product-wiki` pack); read the candidate's `pack.mjs` and `RULES.md` in the canon clone and confirm the fit yourself. - **`site/` states absolute privacy and no-external-asset claims in several places at once — adding any third-party or network asset means re-checking every one of them in the same change.** The claims are not confined to `site/privacy.html`: they also sit in that page's ``, in its lede paragraph, and in the header comment of `site/assets/style.css` ("No external assets, no webfonts, no frameworks"). Landing the analytics beacon updated the page body but left the meta description and the stylesheet header asserting the opposite, so the site shipped claiming "no tracking" while loading a tracker. Before committing a change that adds a script, beacon, font, or any off-origin fetch under `site/`, grep the whole directory for the standing absolutes (`no track`, `no cookie`, `no third-party`, `no external`, `cookieless`) and reconcile each hit — a stale claim in a comment or a meta tag is still a false claim to a reader. --- # Claudinite — where content goes (pack routing) Each pack states what it owns and what it does not. When a rule, doc, skill or check could live in more than one, this table decides it — and "no pack fits" means a new pack or the project's own `local_packs/`, never the baseline by default. | Pack | Belongs | Does not belong | |---|---|---| | `barriers` | directed folder-access graph rules — which directories may never reference which, plus the exceptions each rule allows | where a file should live or naming conventions — that is basics file-placement, not an access barrier | | `basics` | cross-project working discipline, issue-branch-PR lifecycle, repo hygiene, doc/reference integrity and the baseline engineering, testing and debugging skills | technology-specific content — its own tech pack; GitHub Actions workflow or platform behaviour — github-actions; git procedure — git-github | | `git-github` | git and GitHub procedure: commit layering, branch and merge mechanics, squash-merge recovery, PR and merge-to-main commands | the issue-branch-PR lifecycle rules themselves — basics; workflow YAML and Actions runtime behaviour — github-actions | | `github-actions` | workflow YAML and Actions runner platform behaviour: triggers, secrets, permissions, scheduling, artifacts, reusable workflows and their pitfalls | git and GitHub command procedure — git-github; release pipeline content for one product — its release pack | | `grow_with_claudinite` | rules and tasks for capturing lessons into local packs — extraction, dedup, conversation logs, skill-usage folding | repo housekeeping of issues, PRs and branches — that is tidy-repo; cross-repo fleet sweeps are sheepdog | | `html` | hand-authored HTML markup gotchas — element nesting, injected content placement, live browser verification of a page | javascript runtime APIs — web-speech; map widgets — leaflet; npm and dependency policy — node | | `product-wiki` | agent-maintained market, user and competitor research wikis — cited pages, growth logs, the reviewed product-requirements sink | how the product is built or specced — that is spec-driven-product; requirement proofs are executable-requirements | | `tidy-repo` | housekeeping of open issues, pull requests and branches in one repo — triage verdicts, standing trackers, assess-vs-act policy | extracting lessons into packs — that is grow_with_claudinite; Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. - general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. - Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. - statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. 16	- The rule-sync category is nearly all free OSS under 3k stars; the one hosted SaaS (rulesync.dev) is in free beta.

18	- Enterprise scorecard vendors (Cortex, Port, OpsLevel) now sell AI-agent governance from above; OpsLevel's Tidra ships auto-PRs.
19	- The AGENTS.md spec stays minimal by design — no enforcement, versioning, or packaging — leaving that layer open.
20	
21	## The substrate: per-repo convention files
22	
23	Every agent-facing repo already carries at least one plain-text convention
24	file, and Claudinite has to interoperate with all of them rather than compete
25	with them:
26	
27	- **AGENTS.md** is the vendor-neutral standard: a plain-markdown,
28	  no-frontmatter file at the repo root, formalized as an open spec in August
29	  2025 and donated to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) on
30	  December 9, 2025 — alongside MCP and Block's goose, with AWS, Anthropic,
31	  Google, Microsoft and OpenAI as platinum members — citing adoption by more
32	  than 60,000 open-source projects.
33	  *Correction (2026-07-31):* this page previously said "read by 30+ agents,"
34	  citing the codersera guide; that page actually says "native support in 20+
35	  tools," and the "30+" figure appears to have been conflated with Ruler's
36	  own supported-agent marketing. The scale citation is now the LF
37	  announcement (primary).
38	- The spec itself is deliberately minimal — "a README for agents," no
39	  required fields, no schema — and says nothing about enforcement, machine
40	  checks, versioning, or packaged conventions. The only shared semantics are
41	  precedence (nearest file wins; chat instructions override). Enforcement and
42	  packaging are out of scope, i.e. open territory.
43	- **CLAUDE.md** is Claude Code's project-memory file, now a four-level
44	  hierarchy (managed policy / user / project / local) plus path-scoped
45	  `.claude/rules/` files and `@path` imports. Claude Code still reads
46	  CLAUDE.md natively, not AGENTS.md — the docs recommend an `@AGENTS.md`
47	  import or symlink as the bridge. Community best practice still converges on
48	  keeping it under ~200 lines (spot-checked 2026-07-31: the cited guide is
49	  alive and still says this).
50	- **SKILL.md / Agent Skills** became a cross-vendor open standard: Anthropic
51	  published the spec (agentskills.io, Dec 2025), and by mid-2026 roughly 40
52	  tools — OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, VS Code, Gemini CLI, JetBrains
53	  Junie, Block's goose — read the same format. anthropics/skills sits at
54	  ~165.3k stars (verified via GitHub API 2026-07-31). The spec mandates only
55	  `name`/`description` frontmatter; nothing about checks or distribution.
56	- **Cursor** keeps its `.cursor/rules/` directory; Cursor Teams now also
57	  markets "Team Commands" with a team baseline and drift detection — the
58	  platform vendor absorbing single-tool rule sharing natively.
59	- **GitHub Copilot** keeps `.github/copilot-instructions.md` and reads
60	  AGENTS.md; GitHub's own blog mined 2,500+ AGENTS.md files for guidance.
61	
62	None of these substrate formats answer the question Claudinite is for: how
63	the *same* convention, once refined, reaches every repo that shares it,
64	stays current there, and is *checked* rather than trusted.
65	
66	## The platform layer: what Claude Code now ships natively
67	
68	The largest competitive change since this page was seeded is Anthropic's own
69	distribution stack (all verified against current Claude Code docs,
70	2026-07-31):
71	
72	- **Plugins** (announced October 9, 2025) bundle skills, agents, hooks, MCP
73	  servers, LSP servers, and default settings into versioned packages,
74	  distributed through decentralized **marketplaces** (`marketplace.json` in
75	  any git repo/npm source, semver or SHA pinning, background auto-update).
76	- **Plugins can be centrally mandated**: project-level
77	  `extraKnownMarketplaces`/`enabledPlugins`, managed-settings force-enable,
78	  `strictKnownMarketplaces` lockdown, container seed dirs, and claude.ai
79	  org-level plugin sync on Team/Enterprise plans.
80	- **Managed settings** give admins non-overridable org-wide permission rules,
81	  hooks (`allowManagedHooksOnly`), MCP allowlists, model restrictions, and
82	  even an org-wide CLAUDE.md blob — delivered by MDM, machine-wide.
83	- **Hooks** provide deterministic in-session blocking (exit code 2 /
84	  `permissionDecision: "deny"`); Anthropic's own docs route enforcement away
85	  from prose to hooks — validating Claudinite's thesis while shipping the
86	  session-side half of it.
87	- **Native scheduling** arrived in three tiers (session cron//loop, cloud
88	  Routines, Desktop tasks); **auto memory** is per-project learnings that are
89	  explicitly machine-local and never shared.
90	
91	What the native stack still does **not** do — the whitespace Claudinite
92	occupies (absence verified across the plugins/marketplaces/settings/memory
93	docs): plugins converge *clients* (a per-user cache outside the repo), not
94	*repos*; nothing runs convention checks in CI; nothing opens PRs against
95	consuming repos to converge committed files with a canon; and no path exists
96	from one developer's local learnings to a reviewed shared canon. The risk to
97	watch is pace: scheduled tasks, auto memory, and org plugin sync all shipped
98	within about nine months.
99	
100	## Direct rivals: syncing rules across repos
101	
102	The category is crowded, young (almost everything created May 2025–June
103	2026), fragmented, and almost entirely free OSS. Star counts verified via
104	GitHub API on 2026-07-31:
105	
106	- **intellectronica/ruler** (2,833 ★, active) — "Centralise Your AI Coding
107	  Assistant Instructions"; a `.ruler/` directory concatenated into 30+
108	  agent-specific files. Single-repo only. Its README does ship a CI example
109	  that fails on uncommitted generated-file diffs — file-drift checking, the
110	  category's strongest "enforcement."
111	- **dyoshikawa/rulesync** (1,273 ★, 298 npm releases, very active) — CLI
112	  generating configs for 30+ tools from one `.rulesync/` source. Its
113	  supported-tools matrix now lists "checks" and "hooks" as feature columns —
114	  category vocabulary drifting toward checks without shipping enforcement.
115	- **RuleSync (rulesync.dev)** — the only commercial player found: a hosted
116	  dashboard + `rsc pull/push` CLI syncing CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md/.cursorrules
117	  across repos, with a CI-failable `check` command. Free during beta, team
118	  plans "planned." Ranks #1 for the literal query "sync CLAUDE.md across
119	  repos." Unrelated to the dyoshikawa CLI despite the name.
120	- **Goldziher/ai-rulez** (135 ★) — the rival with the strongest enforcement
121	  language: pre-commit hooks literally named `ai-rulez-enforce`, a
122	  `verify` command, and cross-repo "remote includes." All of it targets
123	  config-file integrity, not the code the agent writes.
124	- **agent-sh/agnix** (372 ★, Rust) — a 444-rule *linter for agent config
125	  files* (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, SKILL.md, hooks, MCP) with a CI GitHub
126	  Action. No sync; complementary evidence for the checks-on-config trend.
127	- **yujiosaka/knowhub** (41 ★) — dormant: last push 2025-07-24, two npm
128	  releases ever. The earlier open question about its enforcement is answered:
129	  file-sync verification only.
130	- **lbb00/ai-rules-sync** (35 ★) — cross-repo team sharing via symlinked
131	  central git repos, 12+ tools; npm activity stalled March 2026. No
132	  enforcement.
133	- **fabian-barney/ai-rules** (3 ★) — a content repo vendored via git subtree
134	  pinned to tagged releases; prior art for the vendored-versioned-unit idea,
135	  no tooling.
136	- **Sync AI Agent Rules** (GitHub Action, 1 ★) — compiles layered rules from
137	  a central repo and auto-commits them into agent files; pushes updates,
138	  gates nothing.
139	- **ranyitz/aicm** (36 ★) — closest architectural precedent to packs:
140	  installable npm packages bundling rules/commands/skills/hooks
141	  (`@company/ai-preset`), but outputs are regenerated into gitignored dirs,
142	  and no enforcement or convergence.
143	- Fragmentation is extreme: at least ten distinct repos named "agentsync"
144	  were created Dec 2025–Jun 2026, all under 60 stars — nobody owns the niche.
145	
146	Category-level answers to this page's former open questions:
147	
148	- **Enforcement**: yes-but-narrowly. Five tools advertise CI-failable checks
149	  (ruler, ai-rulez, agnix, rulesync.dev, spxrogers/agentsync), every one
150	  scoped to config-file drift or config-file lint. None runs checks on the
151	  work product, blocks an agent session, or opens convergence PRs. The
152	  sharpened differentiation line: *they check that the rules arrived;
153	  Claudinite checks that the rules are followed.*
154	- **Business models**: except hosted RuleSync, every surveyed tool (15+) is
155	  unmonetized MIT/Apache/Unlicense OSS — an opening, and a price-anchor risk.
156	- **Marketing**: every headline is a movement verb (synchronize / centralise /
157	  share / find); multi-agent breadth (30+/31/20/12+ tools) is the default
158	  marketing axis, making Claudinite's Claude-Code-only focus unusual in the
159	  field. No rival names enforcement in its headline.

182	## From above: enterprise scorecard vendors
183	
184	Internal-developer-portal vendors sell "standards enforced across many
185	repos" to enterprises as **scorecards** (checks graded across a service
186	fleet, with levels and campaign deadlines), and in 2025–2026 every one of
187	them pivoted to AI-agent governance:
188	
189	- **Cortex** rebranded "mission control for the AI software factory" and
190	  ships AI-governance scorecards that check "which repositories have proper
191	  AI instructions" — observation of config presence, not authoring or
192	  convergence. It published Claudinite's exact thesis as marketing: "AI is
193	  writing your code. Who's watching your standards?" (Sept 2025).
194	- **Port** repositioned as an "Agentic SDLC" platform that auto-discovers
195	  "agents, MCPs, skills so you can enforce your standards."
196	- **OpsLevel** markets a portal that "enforces standards automatically" and
197	  spun out **Tidra AI** — the one IDP product found that *remediates* with
198	  auto-PRs across every repo in scope (campaign-driven, not a continuous
199	  convergence-to-canon loop).
200	- **Spotify Soundcheck** (paid Backstage plugin) shipped MCP actions so
201	  Claude Code and Cursor can *query* failing checks — scorecards made
202	  readable by agents, the inverse of governing what agents follow.
203	- The category norm remains observe-and-nudge (notifications, Jira tickets,
204	  deadlines); default-on auto-PR convergence stays ahead of it.

2	
3	Customer profiles and potential users for Claudinite, in three segments:
4	independent developers, small software shops and agencies (2–50 devs), and
5	large enterprises (100+ engineers, platform teams). For each: who they are,
6	what they do today instead, the trigger moment, and what they would pay.
7	Price anchors live in [`Business/`](../Business/README.md); what this implies
8	for the offering in [`Positioning/`](../Positioning/README.md).

10	## Key insights
11	
12	- 90% of developers use AI at work; only ~24–33% trust its output — the adoption/trust scissor is the buying condition.
13	- Claude Code went from ~3% to 18% work usage in eight months with the category's best satisfaction — the fastest-growing agent.
14	- Users file issues literally titled "need enforcement mechanism"; org-wide shared CLAUDE.md is an open 40-👍 request.
15	- Solo devs run dotfiles and symlinks; agencies copy a shared config repo per client — drift machines with no update path.
16	- Indies pay $199–249 one-time for vendored starter files (ShipFast: $250k in 5 months); shops absorb $125/seat for Claude Premium.
17	- Enterprise near-blockers, in order: security review, multi-agent (AGENTS.md) support, private canon — then metrics and SLA.
18	- Spotify's Fleetshift proved the mechanism at scale: 270k+ fleet PRs, 77% automerged — enterprises already hold this mental model.
19	
20	## The market condition: adoption up, trust down
21	
22	- Stack Overflow 2025 (49k+ respondents): 84% use or plan to use AI tools
23	  (up from 76%), 51% of professionals use them daily — while favorable
24	  sentiment fell to 60% and 46% actively distrust output accuracy; 66% name
25	  "almost right, but not quite" solutions as their top frustration. Only 31%
26	  currently use *agents*; 87% of respondents are concerned about agent
27	  accuracy — Stack Overflow's own framing is "agents on a leash."
28	- DORA 2025 (≈5,000 respondents): 90% of developers use AI at work, 80%+
29	  report productivity gains, yet 30% report little or no trust in
30	  AI-generated code. Its central finding: AI *amplifies* existing
31	  organizational strengths and dysfunctions; quality internal platforms and
32	  a "clear and communicated AI stance" are named mediating capabilities —
33	  and AI adoption still correlates with delivery *instability* where control
34	  systems (testing, version control, feedback loops) haven't kept up.
35	- JetBrains (24,534 devs, 2025): 85% regularly use AI for coding but only
36	  44% call it integrated into their workflow; by its January 2026 pulse, 90%
37	  used at least one AI tool at work.
38	- Claude Code specifically: 18% work usage by January 2026 (24% US/Canada),
39	  up from ~3% mid-2025, with category-best satisfaction (CSAT 91, NPS 54);
40	  Anthropic announced $1B annualized run-rate within ~6 months of GA
41	  (Dec 2025). GitHub Copilot leads usage at 29% but has flatlined.
42	
43	The scissor — near-universal use, low trust, "almost right" output — is the
44	condition a machine-enforced-conventions product sells into: human vigilance
45	does not scale with agent output volume.

1	# Business
2	
3	Business models and price anchors for Claudinite: what adjacent devtools
4	charge, which commercial archetypes survive contact with a "plain vendored
5	files, no server" product, and what is genuinely scarce enough to price.
6	Method lessons live in [`Methods/`](../Methods/README.md); who would pay in
7	[`Customers/`](../Customers/README.md). Nothing on this page is a decision —
8	the human-reviewed distillation is
9	[`product-requirements/`](../product-requirements/README.md).
10	
11	## Key insights
12	
13	- Vendored files are trivially copyable — the sellable scarcities are the convergence bot, canon updates, private packs, and SLA.
14	- Governance tooling prices at $19–29/seat/mo (Copilot Business, GitLab Premium); AI-multiplier tools reach $60–200.
15	- pre-commit.ci's $0-for-OSS / $10–100/mo flat org tiers is the closest live pricing precedent for a config-bot product.
16	- Only GitHub Apps can be paid Marketplace listings (95% to publisher) — Actions and plain files cannot.
17	- Spotify sells its paid Backstage plugins only via negotiated AWS private offers — self-serve paid content looked weak.
18	- Sponsorware is hobby-scale: GitHub Sponsors totals ~$100M cumulative over ~7 years across ~70k maintainers.
19	- Behavioral seats (Snyk: committed in 90 days; CodeRabbit: opened a PR) are the emerging norm for repo-attached tools.

60	## Archetypes that survive "plain files, no server"
61	
62	Each with its named precedent and the implication for Claudinite:
63	
64	- **Hosted-service-on-OSS** (pre-commit.ci, Renovate/Mend): the files and
65	  mechanism are free; the *bot that runs the loop for you* is the product.
66	  Claudinite's equivalent sellable: operating the nightly
67	  baselining/convergence fleet and the scheduled agentic maintenance. The
68	  strongest-fit archetype — it prices exactly what is ongoing.
69	- **Open-core / enterprise edition** (GitLab, Mend Renovate EE): core free,
70	  paid tier at org-level controls — scale, reporting, compliance, SLA. Maps
71	  to fleet reporting, private canon, multi-team controls.
72	- **Private-registry pattern** (npm, Docker Hub): public packs free, private
73	  packs paid (~$7–24/user/mo band). Maps directly to "your org's private
74	  canon and packs."
75	- **Support/SLA subscription** (Tidelift): validated as strategic value but
76	  acquired (Sonar, Dec 2024) rather than scaled standalone — treat as a
77	  deal-sweetener, not the model.
78	- **Paid content on a free platform** (Spotify's Backstage plugin bundle):
79	  exists, but Spotify retreated from public self-serve pricing to AWS
80	  Marketplace private offers — read as weak self-serve demand for paid
81	  plugins; enterprise-negotiated deals instead. A warning against "sell the
82	  packs themselves."
83	- **Marketplace billing** (GitHub): publishers keep 95%, but only GitHub
84	  *Apps* can be paid listings — Actions and files cannot. Marketplace
85	  distribution/billing would require wrapping Claudinite's loop in a GitHub
86	  App, which pushes toward the hosted-bot model anyway.
87	- **Sponsorware**: ceiling too low to matter commercially — ~$100M
88	  *cumulative* across ~70k maintainers in ~7 years; mid-tier maintainers
89	  $500–5k/mo.
90	
91	One-time content sales have no working precedent in this space at product
92	scale — though the indie segment does pay $199–249 one-time for
93	boilerplates (see [`Customers/`](../Customers/README.md)), which suggests a
94	one-time *entry* SKU is viable even if recurring revenue must come from the
95	loop.
96	
97	## What the anchors suggest
98	
99	- Per-seat: $10–40/seat/mo is defensible for governance-positioned tooling
100	  (between Codecov's $5 and Copilot Enterprise's $39); the $60–200 AI-premium
101	  band applies only if positioned as a capability multiplier, not
102	  governance.
103	- Flat org tiers: pre-commit.ci's $20/mo (≤25 users) and $100/mo (≤100
104	  users) is the credible low-end floor; per-repo or per-LOC metrics
105	  (SonarQube-style) are the alternative if seats fit badly.
106	- Seat definition: behavioral ("developers whose repos consume a pack" /
107	  "opened a PR in a governed repo") mitigates the uneven-adoption objection,
108	  per Snyk and CodeRabbit precedent.
109	- The free tier is load-bearing in every surviving precedent: free for
110	  public/OSS repos is how pre-commit.ci, Renovate, Codecov and CodeRabbit
111	  all built their funnels.

12	## Key insights
13	
14	- Claudinite's moat is the closed loop rivals lack: enforced checks plus auto-PR convergence plus a measured growth cycle.
15	- The sharpest line available: rivals check the rules *arrived*; Claudinite checks the rules are *followed*.
16	- Hard-coded single-tenant canon, Claude-Code-only, GitHub-only: the three gaps between today's repo and a sellable product.
17	- Versioning is track-canon-head with no pinning or rollback — the opposite of what every winning comparable shipped.
18	- SEO white space is real: multi-repo consistency and enforcement queries rank only blogs; "sync rules" is already taken.
19	- "Context engineering" has the borrowed credibility; "AI-ready codebase" is unclaimed; "rules management" never formed.
20	- The site's mechanism claims all verify against the implementation; its edges (CI-sweep scope, leave-story) are attackable.

22	## What Claudinite actually is (offering inventory)
23	
24	Assessed from the vendored engine and packs in this repository (grounding
25	files cited as `repo:` paths), the product is deeper than the rule-sync
26	category on every axis:
27	
28	- A **spec-validated pack model**: each pack is a `pack.mjs` manifest
29	  carrying always-loaded RULES.md prose, on-demand skills, deterministic
30	  checks split into work-scope (Stop hook, with session transcript) and
31	  world-scope (CI), scheduled tasks, adoption-interview questions,
32	  dependencies and cross-pack contributions
33	  (`repo:.claudinite/shared/engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs`).
34	- **Session enforcement** through four Claude Code hooks, with blocking
35	  findings that hold the session open until fixed and a self-limiting loop
36	  guard (`repo:.claudinite/shared/engine/hooks/`).
37	- A **stateless hourly scheduler** watermarked off the GitHub Actions run
38	  ledger, with exactly-once labeled dispatch issues, dead-claim reclamation,
39	  and outcome ceilings verified in code — hardening born of documented
40	  production incidents (`repo:.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/`).
41	- **Nightly baselining**: deterministic re-vendor of the canon, wiring
42	  convergence, mechanical migrations, one auto-merged maintenance PR
43	  (`repo:.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/baselining/worker.mjs`).
44	- A **growth loop implemented end-to-end repo-side**: conversation capture
45	  with secret scrubbing, lesson extraction, canon dedup, prose-to-checks
46	  conversion, and a skill-usage metrics fold with denominators
47	  (`repo:.claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/`).
48	- **Barriers**: a language-agnostic folder-access-graph engine enforcing
49	  declared isolation walls (`repo:.claudinite/shared/packs/barriers/`).

51	## Strengths (structurally hard to copy)
52	
53	1. **Enforcement depth.** Checks that block the agent's session *and* gate
54	   CI, with what/why/fix findings and reason-required acceptances. Matching
55	   this requires a hook runtime, a two-scope check engine, and a config
56	   model — not a sync script. No rival ships any of it (Market wiki).
57	2. **The convergence loop.** Default-on nightly auto-PRs from a canon. The
58	   enterprise category norm is observe-and-nudge scorecards; the one
59	   remediating product (OpsLevel's Tidra) is campaign-driven, not
60	   continuous. The DIY precedent (cruft's weekly drift-PR recipe) never
61	   productized (Methods wiki).
62	3. **The measured growth cycle.** Sessions → captured logs → local packs →
63	   dedup → canon, with usage metrics. Claude Code's native analog (auto
64	   memory) is explicitly machine-local and never shared; no rival has any
65	   analog (Market wiki).
66	4. **The no-runtime-service trust shape.** Plain vendored files, the
67	   consumer's own CI, every automated change a PR, leave by deleting files.
68	   This sidesteps the ops-cost failure mode of self-hosted IDPs and eases
69	   the enterprise data-flow review ("code never leaves our environment" is a
70	   documented approval accelerant — Customers wiki), and it is a shape a
71	   hosted-registry competitor cannot copy without giving up its model.
72	
73	The unattended-operation hardening (incident-derived dispatch guards,
74	recovery, escalation) is a fifth, quieter moat: it is the difference between
75	a demo and a fleet that runs unattended, and it lives in engine code rather
76	than prose.
77	
78	## Market position
79	
80	- **Against the rule-sync category** (ruler, rulesync, knowhub, ai-rules-sync
81	  and the sub-100-star swarm): Claudinite is the only entrant whose checks
82	  target the *work product* rather than config-file drift. The honest line:
83	  *they check the rules arrived; Claudinite checks the rules are followed.*
84	  The category is free OSS — competing on price is impossible; competing on
85	  the loop (enforcement + convergence + growth) is uncontested.
86	- **Against the native platform** (plugins, marketplaces, managed settings):
87	  complementary today, absorbing tomorrow. Plugins converge clients, not
88	  repos; nothing native runs CI checks, opens convergence PRs, or shares
89	  learnings. The right posture is to *ride* the native layer (distribute
90	  session assets as a plugin; emit SKILL.md-standard skills) while owning
91	  the repo-side loop — and to watch absorption pace (three major native
92	  features shipped in nine months; Peril is the cautionary tale).
93	- **Against enterprise scorecards** (Cortex, Port, OpsLevel): they sell
94	  observation dashboards to leadership; Claudinite sells remediation
95	  mechanics to the repo. Cortex's own marketing ("AI is writing your code.
96	  Who's watching your standards?") validates the thesis and educates the
97	  buyer. Scorecard vendors lack repo-vendored convention authoring and
98	  continuous convergence; Claudinite lacks their aggregation pane — which is
99	  the natural partnership/roadmap seam.
100	- **Category language**: "context engineering" (Karpathy/Anthropic-backed)
101	  is credible to attach to as *context engineering at fleet scale*, without
102	  claiming the term; "AI-ready codebase" is unclaimed blog-tier territory
103	  Claudinite could own; "spec-driven development" (spec-kit, 124.7k ★) is
104	  adjacent but per-feature, not fleet conventions; "rules management" never
105	  formed and should be an SEO modifier only.
106	- **SEO reality** (Market wiki): "sync CLAUDE.md across repos" is already
107	  taken by rulesync.dev; the enforcement and multi-repo-consistency queries
108	  ("enforce AI coding standards CI", "keep AGENTS.md consistent multiple
109	  repositories") rank only blog content — harvestable white space aligned
110	  with the differentiation.

112	## Gaps in the offering (candid)
113	
114	Ordered by how directly they block the customer segments the research
115	profiles:
116	
117	1. **Single-canon, single-tenant hard-coding.** The baselining worker clones
118	   `https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite.git` (must be public);
119	   preferences fetch from that repo's raw URL; fleet enumeration is
120	   owner-affiliation over a personal PAT
121	   (`repo:.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/baselining/worker.mjs`). A
122	   customer cannot point consumers at their own canon without editing engine
123	   code — yet a private canon in their own tenancy ranks #3 on the
124	   enterprise requirements list (Customers wiki). Today "commercial product"
125	   and "one person's public personal repo" are the same object.
126	2. **Claude Code-only.** Rules inject via Claude Code hooks; skills mount as
127	   `.claude/skills/` symlinks; model families are Anthropic-only. Nothing
128	   emits AGENTS.md, Cursor rules, or Copilot instructions
129	   (`repo:.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/converge-wiring.mjs`).
130	   Enterprises demonstrably run multi-tool fleets and converge on AGENTS.md
131	   (near-blocker #2, Customers wiki) — though Claude Code being the
132	   fastest-growing, best-loved agent (18% and climbing) makes this a
133	   defensible *sequencing* choice rather than a mistake.
134	3. **No pinning, no rollback, no release channels.** Versioning is a single
135	   whole-corpus sha stamp always converged to canon head; a bad canon change
136	   propagates fleet-wide in one cycle, gated only by per-repo CI and the
137	   `review` delivery option (`repo:.claudinite-checks.json`). Every winning
138	   comparable shipped pins plus bot-PR updates (Methods wiki); pin-less live
139	   tracking was only ever chosen by operators who owned the runtime.
140	4. **GitHub-only end to end.** Scheduler = Actions cron; dispatch = issues;
141	   delivery = GitHub API auto-merge; no GitLab/Bitbucket story
142	   (`repo:.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/signals/gh.mjs`).
143	5. **No fleet reporting.** Observability is per-repo (Actions summaries,
144	   hook log, tracker issues, a usage JSON). A buyer asking "is this working
145	   across my 40 repos?" reads issues repo by repo. Scorecard-educated
146	   buyers expect an aggregation pane, and the DevEx champion needs an ROI
147	   slide (Customers wiki).
148	6. **The executor path isn't self-installing.** Agentic dispatches assume a
149	   per-repo Claude-Code-on-the-Web routine wired to the `ready-for-agent`
150	   label, which no shipped code creates; without it dispatches age into
151	   `needs-human` (`repo:.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/executor.md`).
152	   Adoption cost is therefore higher than "one conversation."
153	7. **No discovery/registry surface.** Finding adoptable packs means cloning
154	   the canon and listing `packs/`. The content ecosystems (aitmpl at 30k ★,
155	   skills.sh) show discovery is its own gravity well.
156	8. **Platform prerequisites.** Node ≥18 plus bash hooks — native Windows
157	   without WSL is effectively unsupported; monorepos unaddressed
158	   (`repo:.claude/settings.json`).
159	9. **Site-claim edges.** The site's core mechanism claims verify against the
160	   implementation, but four are attackable in a teardown: "the same sweep
161	   runs again in CI" (CI runs world-scope only; transcript checks never run
162	   in CI), "leave by deleting a directory and two hook entries" (it is four
163	   hooks, a workflow, a CI step and a manifest), "one conversation to adopt"
164	   (bootstrap + executor wiring say otherwise), and the generic "AI coding
165	   agents" framing (Claude Code only) (`repo:site/index.html`).

1	# Methods
2	
3	How the industry solved "propagate a convention across many repos and keep it
4	enforced" before AI coding agents existed. These are analogy and lesson
5	sources, not competitors: each system here picked a propagation model, an
6	enforcement model, and a drift story, and their fates predict what a
7	convention-pack product needs. Competitive landscape lives in
8	[`Market/`](../Market/README.md); pricing detail in
9	[`Business/`](../Business/README.md).
10	
11	## Key insights
12	
13	- The winning pattern is pin-in-repo plus a bot that opens update PRs — pre-commit and Renovate both ride it.
14	- pre-commit.ci monetizes exactly Claudinite's loop shape: free for OSS, $10–100/mo flat org tiers for private repos.
15	- Renovate's bot is free lead-gen; Mend charges (~$250/dev/yr) for scale, reporting and SLA — never for the mechanism.
16	- Peril — central org-wide rules, zero per-repo setup — died when GitHub Actions absorbed it; platform absorption kills.
17	- ESLint's flat-config break stranded eslint-config-airbnb: a pack format is an API; breaking it orphans the installed base.
18	- Bare template-sync (cruft, actions-template-sync) never broke 2k stars: the sync mechanism alone is not a product.
19	- GitHub itself gates org-wide enforcement behind paid plans — org rulesets were Enterprise-only until June 2025.
20	
21	## Two propagation archetypes
22	
23	Across nine systems studied, propagation splits cleanly:
24	
25	- **Pin-in-repo + bot-driven update PRs.** The consuming repo carries a small
26	  config with an exact version pin; a bot keeps the pin fresh via PRs.
27	  pre-commit (`rev:` pins + `autoupdate`, and pre-commit.ci's weekly
28	  autoupdate PRs), cruft/copier (recorded template pin + scheduled update
29	  PRs), ESLint shareable configs (semver pin in the lockfile + Renovate
30	  bumps). This archetype dominates *file-based* convention distribution.
31	- **Dynamic central resolution, no per-repo pin.** Renovate `extends` presets
32	  re-resolve from the preset repo's default branch on every run; OPA agents
33	  poll signed bundles from a control plane; Allstar and GitHub org rulesets
34	  enforce server-side. Pin-less live resolution is chosen only where the
35	  operator also owns the runtime and cannot break the consumer's own CI.
36	
37	Claudinite's baselining (vendored corpus converged nightly to canon head via
38	auto-PRs) is structurally the first archetype's *mechanism* with the second
39	archetype's *no-pin policy* — a combination none of the winners chose; see
40	[`Positioning/`](../Positioning/README.md) for the gap this opens.
41	
42	## What the winners did
43	
44	- **pre-commit** (~15.5k ★): a single small config file in the consuming
45	  repo, exact `rev` pins so repos never silently change behavior, and an
46	  explicit `autoupdate` command. Enforcement is local hooks plus
47	  `pre-commit run --all-files` in CI.
48	- **pre-commit.ci** monetizes the loop as a hosted bot: zero-configuration
49	  setup beyond the existing config file, auto-fixing PRs (it pushes fix
50	  commits onto the PR branch), and automated weekly pin updates. Free for
51	  open source; $10/mo personal private, $20/mo orgs ≤25 users, $100/mo orgs
52	  ≤100 users — flat org tiers, identical features across tiers.
53	- **Renovate**: the hosted GitHub App is free with 71,414 marketplace
54	  installs; org-wide adoption is one onboarding PR (it auto-detects an
55	  org-level `renovate-config` repo). Its enforcement is auto-PRs only — it
56	  never gates CI itself. Mend monetizes Enterprise Edition (~$250 per
57	  contributing developer/year, third-party figure) on scale, Merge
58	  Confidence, reporting APIs, and SLA — the mechanism stays free.
59	- **ESLint shareable configs**: registry+semver+lockfile propagation at
60	  enormous scale (eslint-config-prettier ~61M weekly downloads). Nobody
61	  monetized the distribution itself; value accrued to adjacent services.
62	
63	Four traits recur across the winners: a single small file in the consuming
64	repo; near-zero-effort adoption (zero-config or an auto-generated onboarding
65	PR); drift handled by bots opening PRs, not by humans; CI-fail enforcement
66	softened by autofix.
67	
68	## Cautionary tales
69	
70	- **Peril** (hosted Danger: centrally-stored org-wide Dangerfiles, zero
71	  per-repo setup — the closest structural ancestor to a convention canon)
72	  went to maintenance mode after its creator concluded "80% of Peril is
73	  available today in GitHub Actions." Central-rules products die when the
74	  platform absorbs their mechanism.
75	- **GitHub required workflows** were killed and folded into repository
76	  rulesets within roughly a year (GA October 2023) — platform-native
77	  enforcement primitives churn, which cuts both ways for anyone building on
78	  them.
79	- **The ESLint flat-config migration** stranded the ecosystem's flagship
80	  convention package: eslint-config-airbnb never shipped flat-config support
81	  and its TypeScript companion was archived May 2025, handing the installed
82	  base to forks and shims. A pack format is an API; a breaking format change
83	  can orphan every consumer.
84	- **Copy-based template sync stayed niche**: cruft (~1.6k ★) ships `cruft
85	  check` for CI drift detection and a README recipe for a weekly
86	  drift-PR workflow — literally Claudinite's baselining loop as a DIY recipe
87	  since ~2020 — and actions-template-sync (~327 ★) does scheduled
88	  merge-upstream PRs. Neither broke out. The sync mechanism alone, without
89	  curated content and enforcement, is not a product.
90	- **copier** has the most sophisticated drift-merge algorithm in the family
91	  (regenerate old template, diff to extract local changes, re-apply over the
92	  new template, inline conflict markers) — sophistication that still didn't
93	  buy adoption (~3.5k ★).
94	
95	## Enforcement-model spectrum
96	
97	- **Advisory graduated**: Danger's fail/warn/message levels (~5.5k ★, never
98	  commercialized) — the graduated blocking-vs-advisory distinction is the
99	  design export, matching Claudinite's blocking/advisory severities.
100	- **Settings-not-content**: OpenSSF Allstar (org-wide GitHub policy app,
101	  log → auto-issue → auto-fix ladder) and GitHub org rulesets enforce
102	  *platform settings and required checks*, never file content inside repos.
103	  Org rulesets were Enterprise-only until June 16, 2025 (then extended to
104	  Team plans) — GitHub prices org-wide enforcement as a premium.
105	- **Fallback-without-copying**: GitHub's default community health files
106	  (org-level `.github` repo applies wherever a repo lacks its own copy) —
107	  zero drift by construction but limited to a fixed whitelist of file types.
108	- **Runtime pull**: OPA distributes signed, versioned policy bundles agents
109	  poll and activate atomically — a control-plane convergence loop
110	  structurally identical to canon→repos, at runtime instead of via git.
111	  conftest pushes/pulls the same bundles through OCI registries — an
112	  emerging "policy packs as OCI artifacts" distribution norm.
113	- **URL-inheritance + autofix**: MegaLinter's remote `EXTENDS` config merge
114	  plus APPLY_FIXES delivered as commit or PR.
115	
116	## Lessons for a convention-pack product
117	
118	Read directly off the corpus: pinned versions with bot-opened update PRs as
119	the drift mechanism (not silent head-tracking); one-command or zero-config
120	adoption; CI-fail enforcement paired with autofix to keep friction low;
121	free-for-OSS plus flat private tiers or per-dev enterprise pricing; treat the
122	pack format as a stable API; and expect the platform (GitHub, Anthropic) to
123	absorb any mechanism that isn't paired with curated, maintained content.
